paras: The reported lynching near Dongola, Illinois, was a September 1881 wire story that a mob in Union County had hanged a man accused of whipping a child to death. Local Illinois papers instead reported that the accused, Samuel Hazel, escaped after the death of six-year-old Mollie Dalton, and a reward notice and pursuit reports placed him alive and at large into October. Local editors dwelt on the cruelty of the killing and blamed the county's citizens for the escape.

According to the Jonesboro Gazette, as reprinted in the Cairo Bulletin, the killing took place at the house of Nancy Keller in a "rugged portion" of Union County six miles east of Dongola. Present that night, August 31, were Keller, William Hazel, his brother Samuel, and Elizabeth Dalton with her daughter Mollie.

The Gazette's account said Samuel Hazel beat the child with a cowhide for an hour and a half because she cried, then kicked and stamped on her until she was unconscious, and that she died about 5 a.m. on Thursday, September 1. A Dongola correspondent of the Cairo Bulletin, writing on August 31, gave the same core facts and reported that "the murderer has skipped."

A dispatch dated Anna, September 3, told a different story: a child near "Gongola," nine miles south of Anna, had been whipped to death, and "it is said" the fleeing murderer was caught and hanged by "an infuriated mob" the night before; the Cairo Bulletin printed the same rumor. The dispatch said an appeal for help had reached Anna and that Deputy Sheriff Baggott had gone to the scene with a posse, and it gave the murderer's name as "said to be Goshirt."

On September 5, Sheriff Henry Rendleman of Union County announced a citizens' reward and an expected $200 from the governor for the arrest of Samuel Hazel, with a full description of him. William Hazel, who had been present at the beating, was reported in jail. The Cairo Bulletin noted on October 2 a rumor that Hazel had been captured in Kentucky. On October 10 it reported him still free in Johnson County, where a posse from Vienna had failed to take him and the county sheriff had met him but not arrested him, considering him "a very desperate man."
No report of a confirmed hanging, an inquest on a lynching victim, or a trial of Hazel appears in the coverage.

The lynching story traveled through national news summaries as a single hedged line, that a man who whipped a neighbor's child "is reported to have been lynched by a mob," in papers from Wilmington, Delaware, to Savannah, Georgia. The Wilmington Daily Republican placed it at "Chattanooga, Illinois," directly beneath an item on a hanging at Chattanooga. The Wheeling Daily Intelligencer headlined the Anna dispatch "Child-Murderer Lynched" although its text rested on "it is said."

As the item was rewritten, the hedge sometimes fell away. The Eaton Democrat of Ohio said flatly that "Goshirt" had whipped "his child" to death and was caught and hanged, and the Claiborne Guardian of Louisiana reported on September 14 that the man "was hauged by a mob."

Papers in southern Illinois told the story as a child murder and an escape rather than a lynching. The Cairo Bulletin's correspondent called Hazel "the brute" and added that no one had "heard of a murderer being convicted in Union county," while the Jonesboro Gazette said his escape "in broad daylight" did not "speak well" of local citizens. From mid-September to late October this version, with the sheriff's reward, ran under headlines such as "A Most Brutal Child Murder" and "the Murderer Allowed to Escape" in Illinois and Wisconsin papers. None of the papers mentioned race.

The Anna dispatch is the only source for the hanging, and it presented the report as hearsay. Against it stand the local correspondent's report of the escape, the sheriff's reward notice of September 5, and pursuit reports as late as October 10, all of which treat the accused as living. Only the Anna dispatch called the accused "Goshirt"; local reports named him Samuel Hazel (once "Hazen").

reader.title: Reported lynching near Dongola, Illinois (1881)
bases: Wire reports from Anna said a mob hanged the man accused of whipping a child to death near Dongola (A5, A1), but local papers reported the accused, Samuel Hazel, escaped and was still being hunted in October (A2, A11, A18); the race of no one involved is stated.

The only report of a hanging was an Anna dispatch hedged as 'it is said' (A5, A3); the local Cairo and Union County accounts, the sheriff's reward notice and pursuit reports through October 10 show the accused at large (A2, A8, A11, A15, A18), which is better evidence than the unconfirmed wire rumor.
The wire rumor of a mob hanging (A5, A3) is contradicted by local reports that the accused escaped and was pursued for weeks afterward (A2, A11, A13, A18).

framing.detail: National news summaries ran a one-line item that the man 'is reported to have been lynched by a mob,' and some rewrites dropped the hedge.
The Wheeling Daily Intelligencer headlined the Anna dispatch 'Child-Murderer Lynched' though its text said only 'it is said.'
Illinois papers called Hazel a 'brute,' 'fiend' and 'demon' and criticized Union County for letting him escape and for failing to convict murderers.

info: The child was beaten on the night of August 31 and died about 5 a.m., Thursday, September 1, 1881, per the Jonesboro Gazette; the Anna wire said 'yesterday' (Sept. 2) and a Cairo item said Tuesday; the reported hanging was put on the night of September 2.
The house of Nancy Keller, six miles east of Dongola (local); 'near Gongola, nine miles south' of Anna (wire).

Of the murder: Mollie Dalton, six, daughter of Elizabeth Dalton. Of the reported lynching: the accused, named 'Goshirt' in the Anna wire and Samuel Hazel in local reports; local reports show Hazel alive and at large.
Accused of beating Mollie Dalton to death with a cowhide and kicking her; the wire said he 'whipped' the child to death.
Wire: 'an infuriated mob' (A5) or 'an infuriated crowd' (A3), unnamed and of unstated size.

As of October 10 Hazel was at large in Johnson County; a Vienna posse had failed to take him and the Johnson County sheriff had met him but not arrested him. A rumor of his capture in Kentucky ran on October 2.
